Sound lab: hear one missile's whole flight

Sound starts with your first click. Every missile has its own sound, built from published data on it: the launcher and how it opens, each motor's burn time, size, thrust, nozzles, propellant and steering, and the engine it cruises on. Mk 41, Sylver, K-VLS and MİDLAS cells open a motor-driven hatch just before the motor lights; UKSK's armoured covers take 2.5 s on hydraulics before a Kalibr, Oniks, BrahMos or Zircon leaves. Hot launches crack the cover and roar out of the uptake; cold launches (HHQ-9, HHQ-16, YJ-21, 9M96, the S-300F, Oniks and BrahMos) are thrown up by a gas charge and light 15–30 m up with a sharper crack; CAMM is pushed out by a piston and puffs itself over. Canister rounds release their cover, then the booster fires. SM-6's four-nozzle booster, the jet vanes of ESSM and HHQ-9, RAM's roll and Kalibr's grid-finned booster each colour the roar; dual-pulse motors (Barak-8, Hisar, PL-15) go quiet and relight; Aster fires its side thrusters just before the intercept. Cruise engines are voiced from their real spool speeds: the turbojets (Harpoon's J402, the TRI-40 in Exocet and NSM, Atmaca's KTJ-3200) whine, the turbofans (Tomahawk, LRASM, Kalibr, Kh-35) hum and whistle, Oniks and BrahMos roar on ramjets. A supersonic missile is silent until its shock reaches you. Penetrating warheads crash through the hull and go off inside a moment later; air-to-air missiles leave a rail with a scrape or drop from an ejector before they light. Variants that share a motor and launcher (ESSM Block 1 and 2, Aster 30 and Aster 30 B1NT) sound the same, as they do in reality. Use the Sound lab to hear any of them. Listening from the camera is true to life: sound fades with distance, loses its highs in the air and arrives at the speed of sound; pausing freezes it. The whole-view setting lets you hear the part of the battle you are looking at from any zoom. M mutes.

Fleets are as of September 2026, with your two changes. The five Reshef corvettes are still under construction in reality (first delivery around 2028), so their loadout here is my estimate. Which three Sa'ar 4.5s stay is also my pick. INS Lahav is in the shipyard and TCG İzmir isn't commissioned, so both are left out. Turkey commits about two-thirds of its surface fleet and 6 of its 12 submarines, holding the rest for the Aegean and Black Sea. Israel also gets three coastal radar sites (Rosh HaNikra, Mount Carmel, Ashdod) feeding its datalink, plus shore-based jammers that degrade Turkish missile seekers and TB3 data links near the coast. No land-based aircraft or missiles are used. Drakon's missiles are hypothetical and given a terminal seeker so they can hit moving ships. The TF-2000 carries a modern layered fit: 32 Siper Block 2 (150 km) outer, 64 quad-packed ESSM Block 2 (active seeker, 50 km) middle, and 32 Hisar-RF (40 km) inner, across 32 fire-control channels, plus 16 Atmaca and two Gökdeniz guns. Siper, Hisar-RF and the Akdoğan ramjet missile are Turkish programs still in development, so their values are estimates. Dolphin submarines here carry the conventional Popeye Turbo cruise missile, not the nuclear version. World mode lets you pick any two navies and a force size; the fleets, air wings and submarines are generated from a catalogue of real classes, with weapon fits from public sources. Ballistic missiles (Drakon's SLBMs and Air LORA) are not guaranteed hits: successive defensive layers each get a shot, every interceptor has only a small chance against them, and a leaker can still miss in the terminal dive. Aircraft use cruise or dash speeds (F-15I about Mach 1.6, F-35I about Mach 1.2, Kızılelma about Mach 0.9). Warships treat aircraft as a last-resort target: they only engage them inside about 25 km, with short-range cells, and never while missiles are inbound. The F-35I is the Israeli-modified Adir rather than a standard F-35A: its Israeli electronic warfare and mission systems are modelled as a lower radar signature and much stronger self-protection jamming. Each hit picks an impact point (waterline, machinery, magazine, superstructure, deck or a glancing blow) and scales with the weapon's impact speed, so a Mach 5 ballistic strike does far more than a subsonic sea-skimmer. Waterline hits start progressive flooding, machinery hits cripple speed, superstructure hits take the radar out, and magazine hits usually finish the ship. Damage is otherwise modelled by hull size: one hit destroys any small craft, about one hit in six causes a magazine or engine-room fire that doubles the damage, a ballistic warhead does roughly double the harm of a sea-skimmer against a large hull, and a ship below 45% hull is mission-killed (weapons offline, barely making way). A carrier's flight deck is wrecked by any ballistic hit. Costs are rough public-domain unit prices in US dollars and are only meant to give a sense of scale. Interceptor hit rates are best against subsonic sea-skimmers and drones and much worse against evasive or ballistic targets. Modern sea-skimmers (Gabriel Mk5, Atmaca and Popeye Turbo) fly a weaving terminal approach, which makes them harder to intercept in the last few kilometres. Each F-35I also carries two Python-5 short-range missiles for close combat, inside its bays with four Sky Sting (six internal stations; internal Python-5 carriage is an assumption). Fighters fly a beyond-visual-range game: they hold CAP stations and commit on threats, shoot at doctrine ranges set by their missile's real envelope (closer in against a jet that can turn and run), crank off the nose to keep supporting the shot, and pump cold to beat a threat. Against an incoming missile they drag it at full power, then beam it with chaff, then break at the last moment; a missile fired from long range bleeds speed and can be outrun, and it loses accuracy if its launching aircraft is shot down or turns away before it goes active. Inside about 15 km, fighters carrying short-range missiles merge and turn with the enemy. Jets watch their fuel and go home at joker or bingo. Turkey's MUGEM carrier and the Kızılelma fighter are future programs, and the forces here are a guess: a 30-aircraft carrier wing (18 Kızılelma, 8 Hürjet, 4 TB3) plus 10 land-based TF KAAN fifth-generation fighters, each with 6 Gökdoğan and 2 short-range Bozdoğan missiles. Sky Sting is a hypothetical Israeli long-range air-to-air missile and Air LORA is an air-launched ballistic missile; both use estimated values. The Dakar class and its 8 SLBMs are also hypothetical. Both boats' SLBMs are modelled as a stretched two-stage Naval LORA (about 9.6 m, some 2,500 km reach), fired from tubes in the sail: the hatch opens, the round is thrown up through the water, broaches, lights just above the surface and climbs away. The TF-2000 destroyer is a future Turkish design and is not in service; its fit here (8-channel Siper long-range SAMs, Hisar-D, Atmaca, two Gökdeniz guns) is an estimate. Missile speeds use published figures (Barak-8 about Mach 2, ESSM about Mach 4, Harpoon and Atmaca about Mach 0.85). Salvo rates reflect each system: C-Dome fires a cell every quarter second and guides many rounds at once, while illuminator-guided systems like SM-1 and Sea Sparrow are limited to a few targets at a time. Kill probabilities are notional open-source estimates, and every run rolls the dice again. Drag any ship or submarine to reposition it, before the battle or during it. Moving units before you press Start also recalculates each side's coordinated strike timing.

3D view & controls

World battles. Theatres use real coastlines (Natural Earth), so fleets route around land, and the starting distance is as far as open water along the theatre allows. Each task group sails in a screen around its carrier or flagship: it closes until its main anti-ship missile is in reach and holds there on slow legs across the threat axis; once its anti-ship cells are empty it opens the range, and if the flagship is badly hurt the group turns for home. A ship with a missile in its terminal run turns end-on to it at flank speed, and a badly damaged escort falls out and heads for port. A group does not empty its cells at first contact: it fires a raid sized to beat the enemy group's air defences, waits until every round of it has hit, been shot down or run dry, takes a minute to assess the damage, then re-attacks whatever is still afloat. Each raid is spread across the ships' VLS sections, so two rounds never leave the same section together. Fighters hold CAP stations and commit on threats, shoot at doctrine ranges set by their missile's real envelope, crank to keep supporting the shot and pump cold to beat a threat; against an incoming missile they drag it, beam it with chaff, then break, and a long-range shot bleeds speed and can be outrun. Jets watch their fuel and go home at joker or bingo. Radar cross-section is modelled by aspect: each type has a nose-on, beam and tail figure in m² (the F-35 is about 0.005 m² nose-on but around 0.3 from the side, a Flanker 12–15 head-on), blended by the angle the radar sees, so cranking or running away shows a much bigger target. Stealth fighters carry their missiles in their bays (F-35: six stations, J-35: four PL-15, Su-57: four R-77M in the tandem main bays and two R-74M2 in the side bays), the doors open briefly for each shot and light the jet up while they are open, and anything hung outside (a J-35's YJ-83K, an Su-57's Kh-35U) adds to its signature until it is fired. At 800 km only long-range missiles, aircraft and submarines can reach at first: fleets close at about 25 knots, so a pairing of short-range navies can take the full three hours.

This is a Tacview-style 3D view of the same engagement engine as the 2D simulator: the underlying math (positions, detection, weapons, damage) is unchanged — altitude and depth are not simulated by the engine, so heights for aircraft, missiles and submarines shown here are a plausible visual estimate from each unit's type and current phase, not a modelled flight or dive profile. Hull and airframe proportions come from each class's published length and beam, and selecting a unit shows a lit view of that class's own model. The file is entirely self-contained: it loads no fonts, images or data from the network, so it runs the same offline as online.

Camera. Drag empty water to orbit, right-drag or shift-drag to pan (the sea stays under the cursor), and scroll to zoom toward whatever the pointer is over. Double-click a unit to fly to it, or empty water to zoom in there. Chase locks onto the selected unit and starts about eight of its own lengths astern — dragging then swings around it rather than dropping the lock. Top-down is a bird's-eye plot and Fit reframes the whole battle. Default view is the one to remember: it drops straight back to an overhead plot of the whole engagement, oriented exactly like the 2-D map, and lets go of whatever unit was selected or being chased. Keys: R default view, + / − zoom, F fit, C chase, T top-down, O orbit, space pauses.

What you are looking at. Distant contacts are drawn as flat symbols at a fixed size, the way a debrief tool plots tracks; zoom in and each one grows into its actual model, in two levels of detail. Missiles, interceptors and aircraft leave trails sampled on simulated time, so a track laid down at 64× looks the same as one at 1×; ships leave wakes, airborne units drop a plumb line to the surface, submarines show as shapes under the translucent water, and a sunk hull settles and rolls over before it leaves the plot.

Recording. Every few tenths of a second of the fight is captured automatically: drag the timeline at the bottom to scrub back through the battle in 3D, step frame by frame, or press Play there to replay it — Live jumps back to the running battle and picks the fight back up where it left off. While scrubbing, trails are rebuilt from the recording, so a missile's tail is the path it actually flew. Selecting a unit in debrief shows a reduced card, since only position, heading and status are recorded, not full magazines.
